content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has incorporated a comprehensive set of recommendations for the treatment and care of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) into its consolidated guidelines. These guidelines replace eight previous WHO documents and provide detailed policy recommendations for various treatment regimens, patient monitoring, and care models. 1. Treatment for Isoniazid-Resistant Tuberculosis (Hr-TB): For patients with confirmed rifampicin-susceptible and isoniazid-resistant TB, a 6-month regimen consisting of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. The addition of streptomycin or other injectable agents to the treatment regimen is not recommended. 2. Treatment for Multidrug-Resistant and Rifampicin-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB): Longer regimens for MDR/RR-TB should include levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline (for patients aged 18 years or older, and optionally for those aged 6–17 years), and linezolid. Clofazimine, cycloserine, or terizidone may be included in longer regimens, as well as ethambutol and delamanid (for patients aged 3 years or older). Kanamycin and capreomycin should not be included in longer regimens. Amikacin may be included for patients aged 18 years or older if susceptibility is demonstrated and adverse reactions can be monitored. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may replace it under the same conditions. Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem should be administered with clavulanic acid, which is available only in combination with amoxicillin (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid). Clavulanic acid is not counted as an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. Ethionamide or prothionamide may be included only if bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid are not used or if better options are unavailable. Para-aminosalicylic acid may also be included under similar conditions. 3. Duration of Longer MDR-TB Regimens: A total treatment duration of 18–20 months is suggested for most patients, with modifications based on the patient’s response to therapy. For patients on longer regimens, a treatment duration of 15–17 months after culture conversion is suggested. For regimens containing amikacin or streptomycin, an intensive phase of 6–7 months is suggested. 4. Shorter MDR-TB Regimens: A standardized shorter regimen of 9–12 months may be used for MDR/RR-TB patients who have not been previously treated for more than one month with second-line medicines and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents has been excluded. 5. Monitoring Patient Response to MDR-TB Treatment: Sputum culture, in addition to sputum smear microscopy, is recommended to monitor treatment response in patients on longer regimens. Monthly sputum culture is desirable. 6. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) for Patients with HIV and DR-TB: ART is recommended for all patients with HIV and DR-TB requiring second-line anti-TB drugs, regardless of CD4 cell count, as early as possible (within the first 8 weeks) after initiating anti-TB treatment. 7. Surgical Interventions: Elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be used alongside a recommended MDR-TB regimen for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB. 8. Care and Support for MDR/RR-TB Patients: Health education and counseling on disease and treatment adherence should be provided. Treatment administration options include directly observed treatment (DOT), non-daily DOT, video-observed treatment (VOT), or unsupervised treatment. Communityor home-based DOT is recommended over health facility-based DOT or unsupervised treatment. Ambulatory care is preferred over hospitalization-based care models. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model. Support interventions, such as SMS reminders, telephone calls, medication monitors, and staff education, should be tailored to the patient’s needs and available resources. Material support (e.g., food, financial assistance) and psychological support (e.g., counseling, peer-group support) should be provided to address indirect costs and improve adherence. 9. Evidence and Justification for Recommendations: The recommendations are based on analyses of individual patient data (IPD) from observational studies conducted in various settings. These studies evaluated treatment regimens containing rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, streptomycin, isoniazid, and fluoroquinolones. A 6-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin (REZ-Lfx) was associated with higher treatment success rates compared to longer regimens. The addition of fluoroquinolones improved outcomes, while the addition of streptomycin did not significantly reduce mortality. Drug-induced hepatotoxicity is a known risk with anti-TB drugs, particularly with regimens containing rifampicin and pyrazinamide. The risk of hepatotoxicity between 6-month and longer regimens remains unclear. 10. Conclusion: A 6-month regimen of REZ plus fluoroquinolones is associated with higher treatment success rates and fewer adverse effects compared to longer regimens. The recommendations aim to balance clinical outcomes, patient preferences, and the feasibility of implementation.
